The salt air always tasted like iron and old secrets. Elias adjusted his woolen collar, the damp chill of the Atlantic seeping through the stone walls of the lighthouse. For forty years, he had been the silent guardian of Blackwood Rock, a jagged tooth of granite jutting into the churning grey sea. His world was reduced to the rhythmic sweep of the Fresnel lens, the groan of the gears, and the endless, indifferent horizon.

Tonight, the storm was unlike any he had witnessed. The wind howled like a wounded beast, battering the glass panes with violent fists. Rain lashed against the lantern room, blurring the beam of light that cut through the darkness. Elias climbed the spiral stairs, his knees protesting with every step, to check the oil reserves. The pressure was immense; ships relied on this light not just for guidance, but for survival.

As he reached the top, a flash of lightning illuminated the sea below. Something was wrong. A distress flare, red and desperate, pulsed from the waves.
